title: Kingdom of Prussia
wiki_lead:
The Kingdom of Prussia (German: Königreich Preußen, pronounced [ˈkøːnɪkʁaɪç ˈpʁɔʏsn̩] ) was a German state that existed from 1701 to 1918. It played a significant role in the unification of Germany in 1871 and was a major constituent of the German Empire until its dissolution in 1918. The Kingdom of Prussia took its name from the historical region of Prussia, and controlled most of said region, although it was based in the Margraviate of Brandenburg, and its capital was Berlin.
The kings of Prussia were from the House of Hohenzollern. The polity of Brandenburg-Prussia, predecessor of the kingdom, became a military power under Frederick William, Elector of Brandenburg, known as "The Great Elector". As a kingdom, Prussia continued its rise to power, especially during the reign of Frederick the Great. He was instrumental in starting the Seven Years' War (1756–1763), holding his own against Austria, Russia, France and Sweden and establishing Prussia's dominant role among the German states, as well as establishing the country as a European great power through the victories of the powerful Prussian Army. Prussia made attempts to unify all the German states (excluding the German cantons in Switzerland) under its rule, and whether Austria would be included in such a unified German domain became an ongoing question. After the Napoleonic Wars led to the creation of the German Confederation, the issue of unifying the German states caused the German revolutions of 1848–1849, with representatives from all states attempting to unify under their own constitution. Attempts to create a federation remained unsuccessful and the German Confederation collapsed in 1866 when the Austro-Prussian War ensued between its two most powerful member states.
Prussia was subsequently the driving force behind establishing in 1866 the North German Confederation, transformed in 1871 into the unified German Empire and considered the earliest continual legal predecessor of today's Federal Republic of Germany. The North German Confederation was seen as more of an alliance of military strength in the aftermath of the Austro-Prussian War but many of its laws were later used in the German Empire. The German Empire successfully unified all of the German states aside from Austria and Switzerland under Prussian hegemony due to the defeat of Napoleon III in the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–1871. The war united all the German states against a common enemy, and with the victory came an overwhelming wave of nationalism, which changed the opinions of some of those who had been against unification.
With the German Revolution of 1918–1919, the Kingdom of Prussia was transformed into the Free State of Prussia. Prussia as a whole was abolished in 1947.

grok_lead: The Kingdom of Prussia was a major European state formed by the elevation of the Duchy of Prussia, held by the Hohenzollern dynasty in personal union with Brandenburg since 1618, to kingdom status in 1701 when Elector Frederick III crowned himself Frederick I "in" Prussia at KÃ¶nigsberg, with imperial recognition secured through support for Habsburg Emperor Leopold I in the War of the Spanish Succession. This dual foundation in fragmented territories east and west of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth positioned Prussia as a rising power despite its non-contiguous lands and modest resources, relying on administrative centralization and military discipline to overcome geographic vulnerabilities. Under Frederick William I (r. 1713â1740), known as the "Soldier King," Prussia underwent rigorous military reforms that doubled the army's size to over 80,000 men by conscripting one in eight adult males via the canton system, establishing a professional force that emphasized drill, obedience, and frugality, which enabled survival and expansion despite limited population and economy. His son, Frederick II (the Great, r. 1740â1786), leveraged this machinery for aggressive territorial gains, seizing Silesia in the War of the Austrian Succession (1740â1748) against Habsburg claims and defending it in the Seven Years' War (1756â1763), while participating in the First Partition of Poland (1772) to acquire West Prussia, connecting Brandenburg to East Prussia and adding Royal Prussia's ports and Catholic populations. These conquests transformed Prussia into a first-rank power, with its army comprising nearly 3% of the population by mid-century, fostering a culture of martial efficiency that prioritized state service over feudal privileges. Prussia's subsequent history featured resilience against Napoleonic occupation, which prompted further reforms in merit-based bureaucracy and universal conscription under Stein and Hardenberg, territorial compensation at the Congress of Vienna (1815) including the Rhineland and Westphalia, and under Otto von Bismarck's leadership (1862â1890), victories in the wars against Denmark (1864), Austria (1866), and France (1870â1871) that expelled Austrian influence from German affairs, annexed northern states, and culminated in the proclamation of the German Empire at Versailles with Prussian King Wilhelm I as emperor. As the dominant force within the Empire, Prussia embodied conservative authoritarianism through its Junker nobility, three-class electoral system favoring landowners, and centralized governance from Berlin, yet its dissolution came abruptly in November 1918 amid military collapse and revolution, with King Wilhelm II's abdication ending the Hohenzollern monarchy and converting it into the Free State of Prussia within the Weimar Republic. This trajectory highlights Prussia's causal role in German unification via realpolitik and military prowess, though its legacy includes debates over inherent militarism contributing to later conflicts.
